Predictive Modeling with Linear Regression Project: ReCell¶

Problem Statement¶

Business Context¶

Buying and selling used phones and tablets used to be something that happened on a handful of online marketplace sites. But the used and refurbished device market has grown considerably over the past decade, and a new IDC (International Data Corporation) forecast predicts that the used phone market would be worth $52.7bn by 2023 with a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 13.6% from 2018 to 2023. This growth can be attributed to an uptick in demand for used phones and tablets that offer considerable savings compared with new models.

Refurbished and used devices continue to provide cost-effective alternatives to both consumers and businesses that are looking to save money when purchasing one. There are plenty of other benefits associated with the used device market. Used and refurbished devices can be sold with warranties and can also be insured with proof of purchase. Third-party vendors/platforms, such as Verizon, Amazon, etc., provide attractive offers to customers for refurbished devices. Maximizing the longevity of devices through second-hand trade also reduces their environmental impact and helps in recycling and reducing waste. The impact of the COVID-19 outbreak may further boost this segment as consumers cut back on discretionary spending and buy phones and tablets only for immediate needs.

Objective¶

The rising potential of this comparatively under-the-radar market fuels the need for an ML-based solution to develop a dynamic pricing strategy for used and refurbished devices. ReCell, a startup aiming to tap the potential in this market, has hired you as a data scientist. They want you to analyze the data provided and build a linear regression model to predict the price of a used phone/tablet and identify factors that significantly influence it.

Data Description¶

The data contains the different attributes of used/refurbished phones and tablets. The data was collected in the year 2021. The detailed data dictionary is given below.

  • brand_name: Name of manufacturing brand
  • os: OS on which the device runs
  • screen_size: Size of the screen in cm
  • 4g: Whether 4G is available or not
  • 5g: Whether 5G is available or not
  • main_camera_mp: Resolution of the rear camera in megapixels
  • selfie_camera_mp: Resolution of the front camera in megapixels
  • int_memory: Amount of internal memory (ROM) in GB
  • ram: Amount of RAM in GB
  • battery: Energy capacity of the device battery in mAh
  • weight: Weight of the device in grams
  • release_year: Year when the device model was released
  • days_used: Number of days the used/refurbished device has been used
  • normalized_new_price: Normalized price of a new device of the same model in euros
  • normalized_used_price: Normalized price of the used/refurbished device in euros

Problem Statement¶

There are a wide range of both numerical and qualitative variables. I need to find the most efficient predictor model for a phone's resale price on the used market.

Observations¶

Data Description

There are 3454 entries in this dataset with 14 variables. There are 4 categorical variables: brand name, operating system (os), 4g, and 5g. The latter two are binary (yes/no). There are 10 quantitative variables: screen_size, main_camera_mp, selfie_camera_mp, int_memory, ram, battery, weight, release_year, days_used, normalized_used_price, and normalized_new_price.

Data Summary

Our target variable is normalized_used_price. The normalized mean price (in Euros) is €4.364712 with a range from €1.53687 to €6.619433. The other numeric variables will be described in the exploratory data analysis section. The wide range of phone brands means that the most common brand is "others". The most common os is Android and the most common cell service is 4g.

Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)¶

  • The goal of this EDA is to understand the data, both as individual variables and in relation to each other.
  • The following questions will be addressed:
    • What does the distribution of normalized used device prices look like?
    • What percentage of the used device market is dominated by Android devices?
    • The amount of RAM is important for the smooth functioning of a device. How does the amount of RAM vary with the brand?
    • A large battery often increases a device's weight, making it feel uncomfortable in the hands. How does the weight vary for phones and tablets offering large batteries (more than 4500 mAh)?
    • Bigger screens are desirable for entertainment purposes as they offer a better viewing experience. How many phones and tablets are available across different brands with a screen size larger than 6 inches?
    • A lot of devices nowadays offer great selfie cameras, allowing us to capture our favorite moments with loved ones. What is the distribution of devices offering greater than 8MP selfie cameras across brands?
    • Which attributes are highly correlated with the normalized price of a used device?

def histogram_boxplot(data, feature, figsize=(15, 10), kde=False, bins=None):
    """
    Boxplot and histogram combined

    data: dataframe
    feature: dataframe column
    figsize: size of figure (default (15,10))
    kde: whether to show the density curve (default False)
    bins: number of bins for histogram (default None)
    """
    f2, (ax_box2, ax_hist2) = plt.subplots(
        nrows=2,  # Number of rows of the subplot grid= 2
        sharex=True,  # x-axis will be shared among all subplots
        gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": (0.25, 0.75)},
        figsize=figsize,
    )  # creating the 2 subplots
    sns.boxplot(
        data=data, x=feature, ax=ax_box2, showmeans=True, color="violet"
    )  # boxplot will be created and a triangle will indicate the mean value of the column
    sns.histplot(
        data=data, x=feature, kde=kde, ax=ax_hist2, bins=bins
    ) if bins else sns.histplot(
        data=data, x=feature, kde=kde, ax=ax_hist2
    )  # For histogram
    ax_hist2.axvline(
        data[feature].mean(), color="green", linestyle="--"
    )  # Add mean to the histogram
    ax_hist2.axvline(
        data[feature].median(), color="black", linestyle="-"
    )  # Add median to the histogram

    # function to create labeled barplots


def labeled_barplot(data, feature, perc=False, n=None, order=None):
    """
    Barplot with percentage at the top

    data: dataframe
    feature: dataframe column
    perc: whether to display percentages instead of count (default is False)
    n: displays the top n category levels (default is None, i.e., display all levels)
    order: order of bars (default is None, i.e., sorted by count in descending order)
    """

    total = len(data[feature])  # length of the column
    count = data[feature].nunique()
    if n is None:
        plt.figure(figsize=(count + 2, 6))
    else:
        plt.figure(figsize=(n + 2, 6))

    plt.xticks(rotation=90, fontsize=15)
    ax = sns.countplot(
        data=data,
        x=feature,
        hue=feature,
        palette="Paired",
        order=order if order is not None else data[feature].value_counts().index[:n],
    )

    for p in ax.patches:
        if perc == True:
            label = "{:.1f}%".format(
                100 * p.get_height() / total
            )  # percentage of each class of the category
        else:
            label = p.get_height()  # count of each level of the category

        x = p.get_x() + p.get_width() / 2  # width of the plot
        y = p.get_height()  # height of the plot

        ax.annotate(
            label,
            (x, y),
            ha="center",
            va="center",
            size=12,
            xytext=(0, 5),
            textcoords="offset points",
        )  # annotate the percentage

    plt.show()  # show the plot

#Pulling out the numerical columns
num_cols = df.select_dtypes(include=np.number).columns.tolist()

#dropping Year released
num_cols.remove('release_year')

#create a correlation heatmap for the numeric columns
plt.figure(figsize=(12, 10))
sns.heatmap(df[num_cols].corr(), annot=True, cmap = "RdYlGn")
plt.show()

The target variable, normalized_used_price is positively correlated with most of the other variables:

  • moderately correlated with screen_size, main_camera_mp, selfie_camera_mp, ram, and battery.
  • weakly correlated with int_memory and weight
  • strongly correlated with normalized_new_price

It is weakly negatively correlated with days_used.

=================================

N.B.: Correlation interpretation using language is notoriously imprecise. The only accepted convention is that values closer to ±1 are strong and values close to 0 are not correlated. I typically use the following convention:

  • |r|≥0.9: very strong
  • |r|≥0.8: strong
  • |r|≥0.5: moderate
  • |r|≥0.15: weak
  • |r|<0.15: no correlation

    axes[i].set_title(brand)
    axes[i].set_xlabel('') # Remove x-axis label for clarity
    axes[i].set_ylabel('RAM (GB)')

# Hide any unused subplots
for j in range(i + 1, len(axes)):
    fig.delaxes(axes[j])

plt.show()

Observations on RAM by brand¶

The vast majority of phones had 4GB of ram. However, there were a few notable exceptions. 100% of the celkon and infinix phones had less than 4 GB of ram. 75% of Nokia phones also had less than 4GB of ram. At the other end of the spectrum, all Google and OnePlus phones had 4GB of ram or more.

print("Correlations between Battery and Weight per Brand (for devices with Battery > 4500 mAh):")

# Get unique brands from df_battery
brands_in_df_battery = df_battery['brand_name'].unique()

correlation_data = {} # Initialize dictionary to store correlations

# Iterate through each brand and calculate the correlation
for brand in sorted(brands_in_df_battery):
    brand_df = df_battery[df_battery['brand_name'] == brand][['battery', 'weight']]

    # Only calculate correlation if there are at least two rows and sufficient variation
    if len(brand_df) > 1:
        # Check for zero standard deviation to avoid RuntimeWarning
        if brand_df['battery'].std() == 0 or brand_df['weight'].std() == 0:
            print(f"  {brand}: Not enough variation in battery or weight for correlation")
            correlation_data[brand] = float('nan') # Store NaN for no variation
        else:
            correlation = brand_df['battery'].corr(brand_df['weight'])
            print(f"  {brand}: {correlation:.2f}")
            correlation_data[brand] = round(correlation, 2) # Store rounded correlation
    else:
        print(f"  {brand}: Not enough data for correlation")
        correlation_data[brand] = float('nan') # Store NaN for insufficient data

correlation_df = pd.DataFrame.from_dict(correlation_data, orient='index', columns=['Correlation']).sort_index()

display(correlation_df.dropna())

# Filter out NaN values and sort the correlations from strongest to weakest
correlation_for_plot = correlation_df.dropna().sort_values(by='Correlation', ascending=False)

plt.figure(figsize=(15, 8))

# Create a color map for the bars based on their correlation value
# Normalize correlation values to the [0, 1] range of the colormap
min_corr = correlation_for_plot['Correlation'].min()
max_corr = correlation_for_plot['Correlation'].max()

# Avoid division by zero if all correlations are the same
if max_corr == min_corr:
    colors = [plt.cm.viridis(0.5)] * len(correlation_for_plot) # Assign a middle color if no variation
else:
    normalized_correlations = (correlation_for_plot['Correlation'] - min_corr) / (max_corr - min_corr)
    colors = normalized_correlations.apply(lambda x: plt.cm.viridis(x))

sns.barplot(
    x=correlation_for_plot.index,
    y='Correlation',
    data=correlation_for_plot,
    hue=correlation_for_plot.index, # Assign x to hue as suggested by the warning
    palette=list(colors),
    legend=False # Set legend to False for the same effect as prior usage
)

plt.axhline(0, color='black', linewidth=0.8) # Add a horizontal line at y=0
plt.title('Battery-Weight Correlation by Brand (for batteries > 4500 mAh)', fontsize=16)
plt.xlabel('Brand Name', fontsize=12)

Observations¶

Observation 2059 has missing values in the selfie_camera_mp, ram, and battery columns. Rather than imputing values to this one individual, I considered dropping it from the dataset. However, I will keep it since I am imputing with the median, the missing data should not greatly affect my results.

In [49]:
#Copying the data frame
my_data = df.copy()
In [50]:
# For all other missing values, I will use the median method to fill the missing data
# Impute missing values with the median for numerical columns
#since brand name and release year have an impact on the type of ram, battery size, camera size, etc
# I will replace missing values grouped by brand and release year
has_missing = ['main_camera_mp', 'selfie_camera_mp', 'int_memory', 'ram', 'battery', 'weight']
for col in has_missing:
    if my_data[col].isnull().any():
        # First attempt to fill using median grouped by brand_name and release_year
        median_val_grouped = my_data.groupby(["brand_name", "release_year"])[col].transform('median')
        my_data.fillna({col: median_val_grouped}, inplace=True)
        print(f"Missing data in {col} is {my_data[col].isnull().sum()}\n")

        # Second pass: there are still many NaNs so I will fill with the overall median of that brand.
        if my_data[col].isnull().any():
            brand_median = my_data.groupby(['brand_name'])[col].transform('median')
            my_data.fillna({col: brand_median}, inplace=True)
            print(f"Missing data on 2nd pass in {col} is {my_data[col].isnull().sum()}\n")

            # Third pass: the 10 remaining NaNs will fill with the overall median
            if my_data[col].isnull().any():
                overall_median = my_data[col].median()
                my_data.fillna({col: overall_median}, inplace = True)
                print(f"Missing data on third pass in {col} is {my_data.isnull().sum()}\n")

#

# Verify that there are no more missing values
print()
print("Missing values after all imputation:")
print(my_data.isnull().sum())

Observations¶

Not surprisingly, the imputation of the missing data using the median method has had little effect on the distribution of the data. The only tangible effect has been a small shift of the mean to be closer to the median. This is most noticeable in the main_camera_mp variable since it had the most imputed values based on the brand median. However, even this change appears to be slight.

Feature Engineering¶

Year is not very useful as a numeric variable. However, there are also too many years to create efficient dummy variables. So I will create a year since release. The most recent phone in the data set is from 2020, so I will use 2021 as a baseline. Thus a 1 will be 1 year since the phone was released. Then the original data will be dropped.

Model Performance Check¶

In [62]:
# custom functions imported from MLS 2 for this project
# function to compute adjusted R-squared
def adj_r2_score(predictors, targets, predictions):
    r2 = r2_score(targets, predictions)
    n = predictors.shape[0]
    k = predictors.shape[1]
    return 1 - ((1 - r2) * (n - 1) / (n - k - 1))


# function to compute MAPE
def mape_score(targets, predictions):
    return np.mean(np.abs(targets - predictions) / targets) * 100


# function to compute different metrics to check performance of a regression model
def model_performance_regression(model, predictors, target):
    """
    Function to compute different metrics to check regression model performance

    model: regressor
    predictors: independent variables
    target: dependent variable
    """

    # predicting using the independent variables
    pred = model.predict(predictors)

    r2 = r2_score(target, pred)  # to compute R-squared
    adjr2 = adj_r2_score(predictors, target, pred)  # to compute adjusted R-squared
    rmse = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(target, pred))  # to compute RMSE
    mae = mean_absolute_error(target, pred)  # to compute MAE
    mape = mape_score(target, pred)  # to compute MAPE

    # creating a dataframe of metrics
    df_perf = pd.DataFrame(
        {
            "RMSE": rmse,
            "MAE": mae,
            "R-squared": r2,
            "Adj. R-squared": adjr2,
            "MAPE": mape,
        },
        index=[0],
    )

    return df_perf

Checking Linear Regression Assumptions¶

In order to make statistical inferences from a linear regression model, it is important to ensure that the assumptions of linear regression are satisfied.

We will be checking the following Linear Regression assumptions:

  • No Multicollinearity

  • Linearity of variables

  • Independence of error terms

  • Normality of error terms

  • No Heteroscedasticity

Multicollinearity check¶

In [65]:
from statsmodels.stats.outliers_influence import variance_inflation_factor

## the function below takes the predictors and calculates VIF for each column pair
def checking_vif(predictors):
    vif = pd.DataFrame()
    vif["feature"] = predictors.columns

    # calculating VIF for each feature
    vif["VIF"] = [
        variance_inflation_factor(predictors.values, i)
        for i in range(len(predictors.columns))
    ]
    return vif

In [67]:
def treating_multicollinearity(predictors, target, high_vif_columns):
    """
    Checking the effect of dropping the columns showing high multicollinearity
    on model performance (adj. R-squared and RMSE)

    predictors: independent variables
    target: dependent variable
    high_vif_columns: columns having high VIF
    """
    # empty lists to store adj. R-squared and RMSE values
    adj_r2 = []
    rmse = []

    # build ols models by dropping one of the high VIF columns at a time
    # store the adjusted R-squared and RMSE in the lists defined previously
    for cols in high_vif_columns:
        # defining the new train set
        train = predictors.loc[:, ~predictors.columns.str.startswith(cols)]

        # create the model
        olsmodel = sm.OLS(target, train).fit()

        # adding adj. R-squared and RMSE to the lists
        adj_r2.append(olsmodel.rsquared_adj)
        rmse.append(np.sqrt(olsmodel.mse_resid))

    # creating a dataframe for the results
    temp = pd.DataFrame(
        {
            "col": high_vif_columns,
            "Adj. R-squared after_dropping col": adj_r2,
            "RMSE after dropping col": rmse,
        }
    ).sort_values(by="Adj. R-squared after_dropping col", ascending=False)
    temp.reset_index(drop=True, inplace=True)

    return temp

Observations¶

We can see that adj. R-squared has dropped from 0.845 to 0.842, which shows that the dropped columns did not have much effect on the model.

As there is no more multicollinearity, we can look at the p-values of predictor variables to check their significance

Dealing with high p-values¶

From the regression model, P>|t| is the p-value for each coefficient $βᵢ.

  • For each independent feature, there is a null hypothesis and an alternate hypothesis. Here $\beta_i$ is the coefficient of the $i$th independent variable.

    • $H_o$ : Independent feature is not significant ($\beta_i = 0$)
    • $H_a$ : Independent feature is that it is significant ($\beta_i \neq 0$)

  • (P>|t|) gives the p-value for each independent feature to check that null hypothesis. We are considering 0.05 (5%) as significance level.

    • A p-value of less than 0.05 is considered to be statistically significant.
In [71]:
# the code  below will copy all of the predictor columns present in our current model,
# olsmodel2, and then loop through them to pull out all of the ones with a p-value >0.05
# each column will be pulled one-by-one and the training model rerun since we want to
# be conservative with our estimates

# initial list of columns
predictors = x_train2.copy()
cols = predictors.columns.tolist()

def treating_p_values(predictors, cols):
  # setting an initial max p-value
  max_p_value = 1

  while len(cols) > 0:
    # defining the train set
    x_train_aux = predictors[cols]

    # fitting the model
    model = sm.OLS(y_train, x_train_aux).fit()

    # getting the p-values and the maximum p-value
    p_values = model.pvalues
    max_p_value = max(p_values)

    # name of the variable with maximum p-value
    feature_with_p_max = p_values.idxmax()

    if max_p_value > 0.05:
        cols.remove(feature_with_p_max)
    else:
        break
  selected_features = cols
  return selected_features

Observations¶

  • No predictor variable has a p-value greater than 0.05, so we will consider the x_train3 as the final model
  • The adjusted R-Squared is 0.836, so our model predicts 83.6% of the variance seen in the used phone prices.
  • The adjusted r-squared in the model without collinearity was 0.838 which suggested that the variables we dropped were not significantly affecting our model.
  • RMSE and MAE values were similar from the training to the test data suggesting that our model is not over-fitting.

The rest of the assusmptions will be checked using our final model, x_train3.

Linearity and Independence Observations¶

The scatter plot shows the distribution of residuals (errors) vs fitted values (predicted values).

If there exist any pattern in this plot, we consider it as signs of non-linearity in the data and a pattern means that the model doesn't capture non-linear effects.

I can see no pattern in the plot above. Hence, the assumptions of linearity and independence are satisfied.

Due to the left skew of the histogram, the non-linear Q-Q results, and the signficant p-value of the Shapiro-Wilk test, the results are not normal. More exploration is necessary to normalize the data.

Exploring Data Transformations¶

Normalized new price looks like it is the variable with the least linear shape. However, I do not see a clear pattern to the data, so I am not sure how it can be normalized. I will keep the data as is and note that the distribution of residuals suggest that not all variables are linear.

Final Model Observations¶

  • According to the adjusted r-squared value, our model can explain approximately 83.8% of the variation in the used sales price.
  • For both training and testing data, the RMSE and MAE values are low and similar, indicating that our final model does not suffer from overfitting.
  • The MAPE value suggests that our model should be able to predict the used price of a phone to within ± 4.56%.
  • In conclusion, the olsmodel_final is a good model for both prediction and inference.

Parameter Observations¶

  • Of the predictor variables, the original price has the biggest impact on the used price, with every one unit increase affecting the used prices by €0.44.
  • Of the brand names, Samsung, and Sony all tend to reduce the resale price. Xiami and Karbonn brands have a positive impact on the resale price.
  • Two of the operating systems have a negative impact on used price: iOS and Other.
  • 4g has a positive impact on the used prices, while 5g has a negative impact on the used price.
  • The number of megapixels in both the front and selfie cameras both slightly affect resale price.
  • RAM has a slight positive impact on price.
  • Oddly, weight has a slight positive impact on sales price.
  • Finally, years since release has a negative impact on the sales price, with each additional year lowering the resale price by €0.02.

Business Recommendations¶

  1. ReCell should focus on cornering the Karbonn and Xiaomi resale markets over other name brands. While many do not have a significant positive or negative impact on resale price, ReCell should proactively avoid Samsung and Sony devices. Their lower sales price is likely due to the high volume of these devices globally.

  2. ReCell should actively avoid Apple phones, instead focusing on the Android market, as the iOS system has a lower resale value.

  3. Phones with higher quality cameras and with more RAM should be a secondary priority. These do have a statistically significant impact on the resale price. However, based on the bivariate analysis above, Sony phones are the largest proportion of phones with high quality cameras. Further analysis into the size of Karbonna nd Xiami cameras is warranted, since the impact on sales price is small and may likely be offset if the larger size camera is on a less desirable brand.

  4. While Xiaomi was one of the brands with a strong correlation between weight and battery size, this should not be a concern for ReCell. Our predictive model suggests that if anything, larger battery size has a positive impact on price with €0.001 increase for every unit in mAh on the battery.
